source_read: PDF, pp. 198–209 (all pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; pp. 200–206 checked on 150-dpi renders; Table 1 note letters read on the p. 204 render; Figs 4, 5 and 6 read on 300-dpi crops of pp. 202–203)

claims.overstatement: The core is supported and carefully hedged (second-hand toxicology, the media's selection, figures illustrative). Two parts are not supported as worded: (1) 'and for mephedrone buy ... fell after the ban': the only 'mephedrone buy' screenshots end on 22 and 24 March 2010 (Figs 4–5), before the ban (16 April 2010); only searches for 'mephedrone' are shown falling after the ban (Fig. 6, generated 06/09/10). (2) 'screenshots of relative search volume without numbers': Figs 2–4 carry a relative 'Search Volume index' axis (Fig. 2 to 3.00; Figs 3–4 to 6.00) and the text gives 'doubled' and 'trebling'; better 'without absolute numbers'. One understatement: the author does read Figs 1–6 as suggesting a 'boomerang effect', news of drug deaths causing more interest in the drug including buying it (p. 205), and concludes that news reports precede increased interest (p. 207); the claim gives only his concession, so 'so they do not show ...' reads as the editors' judgment and should be marked as such, after the author's own reading.
claims.note: All other numbers re-found and checked on the renders: window 26/11/09 to one year after the ban; ban enforced 16/04/10; 18 named deaths; Table 1 note letters c (#1, #2, #4, #14) = 4, b (#7, #11, #15, #16) = 4, a (#5, #6, #8, #9, #10, #12, #13) = 7, none (#3, #17, #18) = 3, total 18; 6 of the 7 'a' deaths have other drugs or conditions alleged (#8 has none); retrievals 9,060 and 8,730 (Scunthorpe, men aged 18 and 19), searched 23/06/11; Scunthorpe deaths reported mephedrone-free on 18/05/10, inquest 2011 alcohol with methadone; 14-year-old girl named online 24/11/09, natural causes reported 16/12/09 (bronchopneumonia after streptococcal A infection, as quoted); ONS 6 of 2,747, 2 with mephedrone alone. Smaller points: (a) the paper's ONS reference is titled 'Deaths related to drug poisoning in England and Wales, 2010' (p. 208), so the 2,747 is that report's total, which Forsyth calls drug-related deaths; the claim could name the ONS measure; (b) the Table 1 notes say only 'subsequently reported' without naming the source; the text quotes newspaper inquest reports for several cases and cites the EMCDDA technical report of Dargan & Wood (2011) for the confirmed cases (pp. 203, 206), so 'from newspapers rather than coroners' records' is a fair reading but not stated case by case; (c) the text's statement that Fig. 5 shows co-occurring spikes in 'mephedrone buy' and 'mephedrone death' searches is not borne out by the screenshot, which notes too little search volume for 'mephedrone deaths' and shows a single line; (d) the abstract's 'most Internet traffic' conflicts with the Table 1 note that the counts do not measure traffic or coverage; the claim's 'linked to mephedrone on about 9,060 and 8,730 web pages' is the correct reading.

anchors.extracted: Mephedrone outlawed in the UK on 16 April 2010; Google Trends and News monitored from the first death attributed to the drug until 1 year after the ban; 18 alleged mephedrone deaths identified from online news; the author says the deaths with the most Internet traffic later proved false alarms.

Google News used to filter news stories on 'mephedrone' from 26/11/09 (start of the scare) until one year after the ban, read chronologically; monitoring identified all UK mephedrone deaths reported online; Google Advanced Search ('Mephedrone AND [deceased's name]') quantified online activity per death.

Limitations: one search engine; Google News sources selected by Google (about 4500 English-language sites, full list not public); Google Trends normalised, showing relative volume as a proportion of the highest, not absolute searches; low graphic resolution; depends on spellings and nicknames; the author treats relative timing as more important than numbers.

anchors.locator: Findings › Measuring newsworthy drug-related deaths from online media, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Google News searches 26/11/09 to one year after the ban retrieved 18 alleged mephedrone deaths of named individuals, listed by estimated web articles returned by Google Advanced Search on 23/06/11; returns not restricted to news items; the two Scunthorpe deaths and the Brighton death had the most returns (#1–3); half were teenagers and most female (Table 1: 9 aged 14–19, 10 women).

18 deaths; note c (mephedrone later reported undetected) #1 (9,060, Scunthorpe, 18/M, alcohol and methadone alleged), #2 (8,730, Scunthorpe, 19/M, same), #4 (2,040), #14 (303) = 4; note b (detected, not a factor) #7, #11, #15, #16 = 4; note a (detected and a cause-of-death factor) #5, #6, #8, #9, #10, #12, #13 = 7, all but #8 with other drugs or conditions alleged; no note #3 (2,490, Brighton and Hove, 14/F, ketamine in brackets, streptococcal A infection), #17, #18 = 3. Notes: table excludes suicides and accidental or violent deaths linked to mephedrone (number not given); retrieval counts measure name linkage, not the strength of the link, traffic or coverage. Other drugs and causes are labelled unconfirmed press allegations.

anchors.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (with the quotations after them)
anchors.extracted: Within one month the Brighton death (14-year-old girl, November 2009) was reported in local online newspapers as natural causes (pathologist: bronchopneumonia after streptococcal A infection, Brighton Argus 16/12/09); earlier accounts stayed online and for several months her name was used by distant local, national and international titles (York, Birmingham, Turkey, New Zealand, China) as a mephedrone death; the pattern continued until 16/03/10.

anchors.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 10th, 13th and 14th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Press campaigns cited a 'string of deaths' without toxicological confirmation; ban enforced 16/04/10; one month after the ban (18/05/10) it was reported that the two Scunthorpe teenagers had not used mephedrone; a 2011 inquest found they died from alcohol combined with methadone.

anchors.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 15th paragraph; p. 206, Implications › Do media false-alarms lead to real harms?, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Author: news coverage confirming mephedrone was not responsible was much smaller than pre-ban coverage speculating it was (citing Fig. 6, a news-volume line); cases implicated at inquest also got less coverage; the highest-profile deaths were not caused by mephedrone by later inquests (Table 1), and media interest was greater in alleged harms before the ban than in confirmed cases after it.

anchors.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 1st, 9th and 12th paragraphs; Figs 1–6
anchors.extracted: Searches for 'mephedrone' doubled after the Brighton death (Fig. 1, no scale values); news volume rose on 17/03/10 (Fig. 2, relative index axis to 3.00) and searches trebled by 22/03/10 (Fig. 3, axis to 6.00); the rise in 'mephedrone buy' searches after the Scunthorpe deaths dwarfed that after the Brighton death (Fig. 4, to 22/03/10, axis to 6.00); Fig. 5 (Google Insights, about 1–24 March 2010) shows a single 'mephedrone buy' line spiking with a news spike on 17 March and notes too little volume for 'mephedrone deaths'; after the ban searches and news for 'mephedrone' fell to about pre-scare levels (Fig. 6, generated 06/09/10). No 'mephedrone buy' data after 24/03/10.

anchors.locator: Implications › Do media false-alarms lead to real harms?, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Author reads the Google data as supporting the hypothesis that reports of deaths increase interest in buying the drug and Figs 1–6 as suggesting a 'boomerang effect'; concedes that typing 'mephedrone buy' does not mean intent to buy or starting use, and that Google Trends give neither numbers of searchers nor reasons.

anchors.locator: Implications › Do media false-alarms lead to real harms?, 3rd paragraph; reference list p. 208
anchors.extracted: Cited from ONS (2011): 6 toxicologically confirmed drug-related deaths involving mephedrone recorded in England and Wales in 2010, out of 2,747 drug-related deaths; mephedrone the only drug recorded or detected in 2. The reference is titled 'Deaths related to drug poisoning in England and Wales, 2010'; no definition or registration basis given.

key_findings.correction: Tally re-done independently from the note letters on the render: 4 / 4 / 7 / 3. 'Mostly by newspapers' is an inference: the notes name no source, and the text also cites Dargan & Wood (2011) for the confirmed cases (pp. 203, 206).
The note's 'without absolute numbers' is right; Figs 2–4 do carry relative index values (to 3.00 and 6.00). Fig. 5 reading (one visible line; 'mephedrone deaths' lacks volume) re-found independently.
Could add that the paper's ONS reference is titled 'Deaths related to drug poisoning in England and Wales, 2010' (p. 208).

risk_of_bias.note: High: outcome status from press reports, retrieval counts that the paper says do not measure coverage, and relative screenshots.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. One correction to 'results_show': it says search interest 'including mephedrone buy' fell after the ban; only 'mephedrone' searches are shown after the ban (Fig. 6); the 'mephedrone buy' screenshots end on 22 and 24 March 2010.

missed: No 'mephedrone buy' data after 24 March 2010 (Figs 4–5), so any statement that buying-related searches fell after the ban is unsupported; the same slip appears in the card's interpretation_gap 'results_show' and in the claim.

The analysis field says the doubling and trebling come 'from screenshots without numbers'; Figs 2–4 show a relative Search Volume index (Fig. 2 to 3.00; Figs 3–4 to 6.00), each normalised to its own period, so 'without absolute numbers' is the accurate wording.

Case #6 (Hove) is classed in Table 1 as mephedrone a cause-of-death factor, yet the quoted inquest report says the pathologist thought it unlikely mephedrone alone killed him given severe coronary artery disease (p. 204; footnote 8 notes the report was later amended): 'factor' in the notes does not mean sole or main cause.
